read.sections.0.text.note: Buddhist monument: wording kept respectful and neutral (พระพุทธรูป, สถูป ... องค์, ผู้มาสักการะ). "the 700s and 800s" written ช่วงปี 700 และช่วงปี 800 (the picture says คริสต์ศตวรรษที่ 8–9); check how this reads aloud and whether คริสต์ศตวรรษที่ 8 และ 9 would be clearer throughout. A reviewer familiar with Thai Buddhist vocabulary should check the whole lesson. Second pass, one style for centuries across the course: one century is ช่วงปี 1400 ถึง 1499 (KEY_TERMS); a run of two or more is ช่วงปี 1400 ถึง 1800 กว่า ("1400 to 1800-something": accurate to the end of the last century and keeps the English numbers for the checker); late/early is ปลายช่วงปี 700 ถึง 799 / ต้นช่วงปี 900 ถึง 999; picture labels and year labels use a dash (ช่วงปี 1400–1499). Where the English itself says '15th century' (teachers' notes, picture alt) the Thai keeps คริสต์ศตวรรษที่ 15 next to the years. ช่วงปี 1400 alone (which reads as 'around 1400') and ช่วงปีคริสต์ศักราช 700 กว่า are gone. A native speaker should confirm กว่า reads well.
read.sections.0.text.source: Borobudur is a Buddhist monument in Central Java, Indonesia. It was built in the 700s and 800s. It has stone terraces, walls carved with pictures, and 72 small stupas, or bell-shaped towers. Each stupa holds a statue of the Buddha. UNESCO explains that its levels follow a Buddhist idea of the universe. Many centuries later, people faced a new question: how should it be conserved? A large restoration ran from 1973 to 1983. Indonesia and UNESCO did the work, with help from other countries. The people who restored Borobudur did not build it. It helps to keep these two times apart.
read.sections.0.text.back: Borobudur is a Buddhist monument in Central Java, Indonesia. It was built in the 700s and 800s. It has stone terraces in layers, walls carved with pictures, and 72 small stupas, or bell-shaped towers. Each stupa has a Buddha image inside. UNESCO explains that Borobudur's levels follow one Buddhist idea of the universe. Many centuries later, people faced a new question: how should this place be conserved? A major restoration took place from 1973 to 1983. Indonesia and UNESCO did this work, with help from other countries. The people who restored Borobudur were not its builders. Separating these two times helps understanding.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Borobudur is a Buddhist temple on the island of Java. People built it more than 1,000 years ago. It has stone steps and walls with carved pictures. At the top are 72 small stone towers. Each one holds a statue of the Buddha. From 1973 to 1983, a big team fixed it. This careful work is called conservation. Indonesia and UNESCO did it together. The team did not build the temple.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Borobudur is a Buddhist temple on the island of Java. People built it more than 1,000 years ago. It has stone steps and walls carved with pictures. At the top are 72 small stone towers, called stupas. Each has a Buddha image inside. From 1973 to 1983, a big team repaired this temple. Careful work like this is called conservation. Indonesia and UNESCO did this work together. This team were not the builders of the temple.

read.sections.1.heading.back: An archive made during the work

read.sections.1.text.source: An archive is a set of records kept so people can study them later. During the restoration, the team took photos, made drawings and films, and wrote reports. An office at Borobudur keeps them today. Its list counts 71,851 sheets of photos and 6,043 sheets of as-built drawings and maps. An as-built drawing shows what workers found and recorded during the work. It is not a plan from the first builders. A later conservator can compare a photo with a drawing and ask why a repair was made. In 2017, UNESCO gave the archive recognition. That date is about the records, not the monument.
read.sections.1.text.back: An archive is a collection of records kept for people to study later. During the restoration, the team took photos, made drawings and films, and wrote reports. Today an office at Borobudur keeps these. The office's list counts 71,851 photos and 6,043 as-built drawings and maps. As-built drawings show what workers found and recorded during the work, not the first builders' plans. Later conservators can compare photos with drawings and ask why repairs were done that way. In 2017, UNESCO recognised this archive. That date is about the records, not about the monument.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: An archive is a set of records. People keep them to look at later. During the work, the team took photos. They made drawings and wrote notes. There are 71,851 sheets of photos. There are 6,043 sheets of as-built drawings. An as-built drawing shows what the workers found. Later, people can look at a photo and a drawing. They can ask why a part was fixed. In 2017, UNESCO gave the archive recognition. That date is about the records.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: An archive is a collection of records. People keep it to look at later. During the work, the team took photos. They drew plans and wrote notes. There are 71,851 photos. There are 6,043 as-built drawings. As-built drawings show what workers found. Later, people can look at photos together with drawings, and ask why that part was repaired. In 2017, UNESCO recognised this archive. That date is about the records.

read.sections.2.text.source: The second picture is a photo taken in 1976 by Gerard Bolla for UNESCO. It records a moment of modern conservation work. Look at what is in the photo, then ask what is outside it. A photo cannot tell us what the first builders planned, or why each repair was chosen. It cannot tell us what Borobudur means to every visitor and worshipper. People can add to the record. In 2019, a show of photos by Suparno opened near Borobudur. He worked at the Borobudur office and was trained to photograph the repairs. His memories can answer questions one photo leaves open.
read.sections.2.text.back: The second picture is a photo Gerard Bolla took for UNESCO in 1976. This picture records one moment of the modern conservation work. Look at what is in the picture, then ask what is outside it. The photo cannot tell us how the first builders planned, or why each part was repaired that way, and cannot tell what Borobudur means to each visitor and worshipper. People can help add to the record. In 2019, an exhibition of photos by Suparno opened near Borobudur. He used to work at the Borobudur office and was trained to photograph the repair work. His memories help answer questions a single photo cannot.

He worked at Borobudur and took photos of the work. People like him can tell us more.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: The second picture is a photo from 1976, taken by Gerard Bolla for UNESCO. This picture shows repair work on the temple, not the first builders. The photo cannot show how they planned, and cannot show what this place means to each person who comes. In 2019, there was an exhibition of photos by Suparno. He used to work at Borobudur and photographed the repair work. People like him can tell us more.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Borobudur is a Buddhist place of worship and pilgrimage today. Use respectful, neutral words ("Many Buddhists ...", "UNESCO explains ..."), never rank beliefs, and never ask learners about their own religion; in Speak, "people who come to worship" is a group to think about, not a question about anyone in the room. Preview the video: by UNESCO's account its narration mentions a volcano and describes a carving of the Buddha being tempted.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: Borobudur is a place of Buddhist worship and pilgrimage today. Use respectful, neutral wording ("Many Buddhists...", "UNESCO explains that..."). Don't rank beliefs, and don't ask learners about their own religion. In the Speak step, "worshippers" is a group of people to think about, not a question about anyone in the room. Preview the video: according to UNESCO's account, the narration mentions a volcano and describes carvings of the Buddha being tempted.

educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners keep the ancient monument (built 700s–800s), the 1973–1983 restoration and the 2017 Memory of the World recognition apart, and write an accurate, dated caption with two limits. Evidence move: put the three dates in three boxes on the board before learners look at the 1976 photo. A sound answer gives who (Gerard Bolla for UNESCO), when (1976) and what (modern conservation work), then two questions the photo cannot answer.
educatorNotes.0.back: Goal: learners separate the ancient monument (built in the 700s–800s), the 1973–1983 restoration and the 2017 Memory of the World recognition, and write an accurate, dated photo caption with two limits. Evidence method: write the three dates in three boxes on the board before learners look at the 1976 photo. A good answer says who (Gerard Bolla for UNESCO), when (1976) and what (modern conservation work), then gives two questions the photo cannot answer.

educatorNotes.1.source: Misconception to address: that a conservation photo is evidence of the ancient construction. Source caveats: the archive's numbers (71,851 photo sheets, 6,043 as-built drawing sheets, 425 project documents) come from Indonesia's nomination form on UNESCO's site; the 2017 date comes from news reports of the recognition, as UNESCO's own archive page could not be opened. UNESCO's listing says the temple was rebuilt in two phases in the 1900s, the second from 1973 to 1983; the lesson covers only the second. The back of the 1976 print (Commons file "PHOTO0000003469 0000") carries UNESCO's own typed caption from that time, a source in itself: it calls the work "in progress" and dates UNESCO's agreement with Indonesia to 12 October 1972. Suparno's 2019 exhibition (Borobudur Conservation Office with UNESCO Jakarta) is reported by The Jakarta Post.
educatorNotes.1.back: Misconception to address: that a photo of conservation work is evidence of the ancient building. Source caution: the archive figures (71,851 photos, 6,043 as-built drawings, 425 project documents) come from Indonesia's nomination form on UNESCO's website. The 2017 date comes from news of the recognition, because UNESCO's own archive page could not be opened. UNESCO's listing says the temple was rebuilt in two phases in the 1900s, the second from 1973 to 1983; the lesson covers only the second phase. The back of the 1976 print (the Commons file "PHOTO0000003469 0000") has a caption UNESCO typed at the time, which is a source in itself. That caption calls the work "in progress" and dates the UNESCO–Indonesia agreement to 12 October 1972. Suparno's 2019 exhibition (the Borobudur Conservation Office with UNESCO Jakarta) was reported by The Jakarta Post.
